The eggs of the Short-tailed paradigalla (Paradigalla brevicauda) are relatively small for a bird of its size, measuring 4.1 centimeters in length and 2.7 centimeters in width. From these dimensions, one can calculate an estimated egg weight of approximately 15.6 grams, a value derived using the standard prolate spheroid formula for bird eggs. This modest egg mass contributes to a wet weight at birth for the hatchling of just 12 grams [Wwb = 12 grams], a figure that reflects the species’ altricial developmental strategy. The neonate emerges from the egg after an incubation period of 23 to 24 days. Field observations of nests in the highlands of Papua New Guinea suggest that when eggs are maintained at the average incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the typical age at birth is approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a value slightly shorter than the extremes noted in wild clutches. This incubation regime is critical, as even small thermal deviations can extend or truncate the development window, influencing the chick’s initial condition upon hatching. The altricial nestling emerges blind and largely immobile, relying entirely on parental brooding and provisioning during its vulnerable first days of life. Such a low birth mass places the species at the lower end of the mass spectrum among paradisaeids, a feature that may be linked to the energetic constraints of rearing a single offspring per reproductive event. This investment pattern is a cornerstone of the species' life history strategy.

As the nestling develops under the attentive care of both parents, it undergoes a rapid phase of mass gain and feather growth. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult males ranges from 160 to 184 grams, with a typical central value of 170 grams [Wwi = 170 grams], a mass that is characteristic of a medium-bodied bird-of-paradise. Females are generally slightly smaller, though comprehensive body mass data for this sex remain sparse in the literature. This adult body mass is achieved after a sustained period of growth, and it represents the culmination of the species' investment in somatic development before the onset of reproduction. During the nestling phase, the chick passes through several developmental milestones. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, which correspond to a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time from hatching to fledging is approximately 26 days from hatching [tx = approximately 26 days from hatching]. This fledging interval is relatively rapid for a bird of this ultimate size, suggesting an adaptive strategy to minimize the period of peak vulnerability to predation within the nest. The young bird, upon achieving sustained flight, begins a post-fledging phase of independence, gradually learning to forage for fruits and arthropods in the montane forest canopy. This period of parental provisioning may continue for several more weeks, gradually tapering off as the juvenile's foraging proficiency improves. The fledgling's first flight is a critical transition, marking the shift from a sedentary nest-bound existence to a more mobile lifestyle.

The trajectory toward reproductive competence continues after the fledgling achieves independence. Puberty in Paradigalla brevicauda, marked by the onset of gonad maturation and the development of adult plumage, occurs at 78 days after hatching [tp = 78 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at the same thermal regime at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This developmental schedule is relatively compressed compared to that of many other birds-of-paradise, likely reflecting the species' high-elevation montane environment, where a shorter growing season and the need to secure a territory before the next breeding cycle may place a premium on early maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity is accompanied by pronounced behavioral changes, including the onset of the elaborate courtship displays for which the paradisaeids are renowned. Males begin to establish and defend display arenas, often a cleared patch of forest floor or a low-hanging branch, where they perform ritualized dances to attract potential mates. At this stage, the young adult also begins to engage in the competitive dynamics that will define its reproductive career. The period between fledging and puberty is a critical window during which the juvenile must refine its foraging skills, avoid predation, and gain the body condition necessary to support the energetic demands of display and eventual reproduction. This post-fledging interval, lasting several weeks, shapes the individual's future reproductive prospects.

After reaching puberty, a reproductively active adult does not typically breed immediately. Instead, the first successful reproductive event is contingent on securing a suitable territory and a mate. Once these conditions are met, the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], a delay that is measured in the context of the species' annual cycle at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This first breeding attempt represents a major life-history milestone, as the individual must balance the energetic costs of nest building, egg production, and parental care with its own maintenance requirements. The female typically lays a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], a remarkably low fecundity that is a direct reflection of the species' maximum reproductive rate. Furthermore, the reproductive strategy of this bird-of-paradise is characterized by only one such clutch per year [F_R_i = one such clutch per year], an interval that aligns with the seasonal availability of fruit and invertebrate prey in the montane forests. This extremely low annual reproductive output, amounting to a single egg annually, stands in stark contrast to the high fecundity of many passerines. The species thus exhibits a slow life-history pace, with a single offspring per year representing a maximal investment in each individual nestling. This investment is channeled into prolonged parental care and the production of a large, well-provisioned egg relative to the mother's body mass.

The lifespan of Paradigalla brevicauda provides the temporal framework within which this low-reproductive-rate strategy can be successful. The maximum longevity recorded for this species in the wild is 15 years [am = 15 years], a duration that is quite extended for a passerine of its body size, though typical within the wider family Paradisaeidae at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively long lifespan allows individuals multiple opportunities to breed, compensating for the extremely low annual fecundity of a single egg per year. When maintained at the species' basal active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the total period of reproductive activity can span over a decade. During this time, a single successful female may produce only 10 to 12 offspring across her entire lifespan, provided she breeds every year without interruption. This demographic reality places a high premium on the survival of each individual egg and chick, and it helps explain the intense parental investment observed, including prolonged incubation, vigilant nest defense, and extended post-fledging provisioning. By the time an individual approaches the upper bounds of its lifespan, a period of reproductive senescence may set in, characterized by a reduction in the frequency or success of breeding attempts. Ultimately, the combination of a very low reproductive rate and a relatively long lifespan defines the species' position on the slow end of the life-history continuum, a strategy that is viable in a stable, low-predation montane environment where competition for territory is intense but adult survival is relatively high.
